spoken_segments.text: All right. Uh, there was a moment in January of 2025 when I was just coding.

And I wanted to see what if you just make an agent? This was before Claude Code. And it was like the dumbest stuff ever. It was like, change this background color. But it just blew my mind when I saw an agent
actually work for the first time. It ran commands. It looked at itself. It gave itself its own feedback loops. That blew my mind. And I had this sense, I think
that everyone has when they first see an agent, that everything is going to change after that. Everything is going to change about how you build software. I think we've all felt that. Everything
is going to change about how you form companies to work on software. And how you sell software. How you distribute software, all other work is going to change. And it was just
an absolutely crazy, crazy moment. Um, I was actually at the Frankfurt Airport with Thorsten Ball on our team. Um, he wrote that compiler book, anyone, who knows Thorsten

on our team? Yeah, he's a cool guy. Um, we were just like minds-blown at the Frankfurt Airport and we knew that everything was going to change. We didn't know where this was all going to go, but we just wanted
to go, we just wanted to go run at it. So inside of Sourcegraph, which was a 200-person enterprise software company, I was the CEO.
And we made code search, we decided to just start building this, to tune out everything else, and just start building this thing, not go to sales calls, not go to like exec
meetings, none of that stuff, just tune out all the distractions.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker's recollection of building a primitive agent in January 2025 ('change this background color') and realizing 'everything is going to change' aligns directly with the 'Jan 2025 Amp starts' timeline marker, the 'Everything will change' waveform graphic, and the right-hand terminal screenshot.

spoken_segments.text: And I was in this position that I think a lot of people say, you know, wow, you know, I'm a software developer in a company

and I want to change, I want my company to be more AI-forward and I can't. Um, you know, I was the CEO, and in theory I could change anything, I could change teams, I could say you don't need to get pull requests,
code review. Uh you don't need to you know do any of the other processes we used to do. And yet it was very hard what we did. As we ended up taking 20 people uh from the
company and inside of Sourcegraph still we made a little team, the Amp team. And uh that's what we tried. So for those of you who are trying to push back against your company
to try to make it more agent friendly, I have a lot of sympathy for you and I hope that you can take away some things from here. Um, I know how hard it is and also, have some empathy for your CEO
too, it's hard for them too. This is a really hard kind of change and transformation.

spoken_segments.text: But we knew that there are some things that were going to change. And this all seems kind of obvious now, but back in
2025, early 2025, with this idea of enterprise ready, you do this thing and then you can build a sales team and go sell it. We knew that that was just going to totally die off. You had to be
on the frontier. If you had, you know, a taste of success and then you started doing all the enterprise checklist bullshit to make the median enterprise buyer happy, your
product was going to go obsolete in like three months. And the whole game had to change. Nothing mattered other than making it so that the people at these other companies loved
your product and the CEO, the budget was infinite and all bets were off. So we knew that. We didn't quite know uh all the challenges we'd run into.

spoken_segments.text: Um, also, you know, in this world where agents can build a product or build a feature, how do you even think about differentiation? I mean to this day there's people who say, well why is Amp better? Why
is, you know, Claude Code better than Codex or whatever. And so many people are begging to have the answer in the form of, well, it's these three features, you know, uh Amp has Orbs which are really
good cloud agents and we have multiplayer. But the crazy thing is, you all know that if we can do that and we prove it, then any of our competitors could as well. So, you know, why even play

that game? Like what does it even mean to build and sell software, why would you go and hire a sales team, why would you go and do anything in the traditional way if you don't even know what it's going to look like in a month?
And if you don't even know how to describe differentiation, there's no sustainable differentiation.

spoken_segments.text: So we knew that we just had to change everything, and we rethought so many things, because kind of unintentionally, we were

under some weird constraints. We decided to spin out Amp. So for those of you who have been at a company, at like a small, uh, you know, you're on a small team in a company and you're trying to do things different,

you're trying to be the startup within a startup, you probably have these fantasies of let's just go off and start a new company. Well, we actually did that. We, you know, did the right thing by investors and employees and everyone has

ownership in both, but we actually spun out and for a year until last Friday, we couldn't hire anyone. We couldn't grant options. The legal spin-off process was a huge pain. And we were forced to make do with the 21 people that we brought

over. We didn't have time in this crazy competitive environment to do, you know, we couldn't move as slowly in order to do um, you know, mandatory pull requests. We couldn't have meetings. We couldn't have our time be sucked up by enterprises that would need to take, you know,

many months to sign on something. And so we were forced into this radically different way of working. And we also had this environment where every single person on the team has a huge stake in the company. And

that skin in the game that you get when AI makes it so that you can operate with way less people, skin in the game, it's like this spiritual thing for the soul of great people. It makes them better at everything they do. It makes them grow faster, and
so this is what we have seen. This, I think, when you've seen a company that operates like this without any of that bullshit, it's
obvious how companies like this are going to crush everyone else and how every company in the future is going to look a lot more like that.

scenes.alignment_note: While discussing the spin-out constraints, Quinn highlights items directly from the table: abandoning 'Mandatory PRs', eliminating 'Many standing meetings', and how 'skin in the game grows you' replaces 'Hiring as the fix'.

spoken_segments.text: And the difference is when you can push and you can do it any time of day, just by yourself, you can chunk up your
